content: Marasmus is a severe form of protein-energy malnutrition that is primarily characterized by a significant deficiency in energy intake. It is one of the types of protein-energy malnutrition (PEM), alongside conditions such as kwashiorkor and cachexia. Cachexia is particularly common in developed countries. Children suffering from marasmus appear emaciated, with their body weight often reduced to less than 80% of the normal weight expected for their height. The condition is more frequently observed in children under the age of one, whereas kwashiorkor tends to occur more commonly after 18 months of age. The primary cause of marasmus is an inadequate intake of calories, leading to a severe energy deficit. The clinical signs of marasmus include dry skin and loose skin folds that hang over areas such as the buttocks and axillae. There is a marked loss of adipose tissue from typical fat storage areas, such as the buttocks and thighs. Affected individuals are often fretful, irritable, and exhibit an intense hunger. Additional signs may include alternating bands of pigmented and depigmented hair, known as the flag sign, or a flaky paint appearance of the skin caused by peeling. Treatment of marasmus requires addressing not only the symptoms but also the complications associated with the condition. These complications, such as infections, dehydration, and circulatory disorders, are often life-threatening and contribute to high mortality rates if left untreated. In advanced stages of marasmus, the body’s protein synthesis machinery, which itself is composed of protein, becomes degraded. At this critical point, the condition progresses to a stage of no return, where even the administration of food or protein fails to reverse the damage or prevent death.
